newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Thousands gather to return to Rwanda, U.N. says.
newsitem.headline: Thousands gather to return to Rwanda, U.N. says.

text.p: Some 11,000 Rwanda refugees who say they were abandoned by leaders of the former Hutu army have gathered just inside Zaire determined to return home, the United Nations refugee agency UNHCR reported on Friday.

UNHCR spokeswoman Pam O'Toole told a news briefing the refugees were at two different locations on hills behind the town of Bukavu where a vast camp controlled by extremist Hutu militia existed until last November.
"They appear determined to repatriate. We are trying to provide transport for them, and some have already gone back of their own accord," she said.
"They say they were abandoned in the forests by their leaders from the former Rwandan army after fighting with Zairean rebels."

O'Toole said the refugees were among people who fled U.N.-supplied camps in the region where over a million lived for more than two years after fleeing Rwanda in the wake of a Hutu-led genocide against Tutsis in 1994.

The exodus came after Tutsi-led rebels routed the then Rwandan army and established a new government in Kigali. Many Hutus feared retliation for the killing of up to a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

The people found near Bukavu "are suffering from dehydration and exhaustation, are disillusioned with their former leaders, fed up with being in the forests and want to go home", the UNHCR spokeswoman said.

Last October and November, some 750,000 Rwandan refugees in Zaire went back to their own country after Zairean rebels including local Tutsis took control of much of the region and destroyed the power of the Hutu militias in the camps.
But O'Toole said the UNHCR was concerned over reports that some Zairean rebel elements had been maltreating or harassing the Bukavu refugees.

As part of a bid to locate other Rwandan Hutus who fled deeper into Zaire late last year, she said the UNHCR had been flying over an area near the town of Shabunda where reports said many refugees were hiding in the forests.

Although a UNHCR team could not land, they had seen three separate large groups that appeared to total tens of thousands. The team was on Friday flying over another area where even more people were said to be located.

O'Toole said the UNHCR had made contact with refugees gathered around the village of Tingi-Tingi near Lubutu in eastern Zaire, where some 120,000 had camped, but wanted to ensure they did not think the agency planned to make their camps permanent.
U.N. officials say Hutu extremists are active among these refugees and among an estimated 40,000 more near the village of Amisi to the south.
The UNHCR was adopting a dual approach, the spokeswoman said, by tackling "both the need for emergency aid and repatriation for those who want it".

She said the Tingi-Tingi refugees -- among whom the U.N. Children's Fund UNICEF says the death rate, especially among infants, is mounting because of malnutrition -- had to be fed for their own health and to stop them stealing from local people.

But the UNHCR was looking at how to get back to Rwanda those who wanted to go home and was looking at airlifting a number of unaccompanied children who had been separated from parents who had already returned.
